inline.s: Awareness is the heart of the preliminaries. When awareness grows by one measure, you are one measure more at ease. So seize every opportunity to cultivate awareness. If you meet difficulties in your practice later on, the problem will always be that your awareness is not yet sufficient. Supply the awareness you lack, and the problem will untangle itself at once.
Q: What is a delusive thought? What is right mindfulness?

A: Strictly speaking, whatever is thought is delusive; hence every thought and every notion is a delusive thought, and only no-thought is right mindfulness. Generally, however, a delusive thought means a thought that is unnecessary and should not be there. When you recite the Buddha’s name, for instance, the Buddha’s name is right mindfulness and other thoughts are delusive. When you practice Chan, the huatou is right mindfulness and other thoughts are delusive. When you contemplate the mind, awareness of the present thought is right mindfulness and other thoughts are delusive. When you are aware of your movements, that awareness is right mindfulness and other thoughts are delusive.
Q: If both hands and feet are moving, which one do I be aware of?

A: At the beginning, choose the most convenient point of awareness. When practicing tai chi, for example, the eyes follow the hands, so be aware of the hand your eyes are resting on. Once your awareness has matured, you can be aware of the movement as a whole.
Q: When I am aware of my movements, delusive thoughts still arise. What should I do?

A: This is common among beginners. The cause is that your awareness is neither focused nor continuous, so awareness and delusive thoughts alternate: one moment you are aware, the next moment you are lost in thought, and so the two seem to run side by side. The remedy is this: at the beginning, simply knowing that you are being aware is enough. Practice without letup, and your awareness will of itself become ever more focused and continuous. When your practice matures and your awareness runs unbroken, no delusive thought can slip in. Then, the moment you are aware of a movement, delusive thoughts subside of themselves. It is like a Westerner who comes to China and must eat with chopsticks. At first he is hopelessly clumsy, but he need only hold to one rule: when eating, chopsticks must be used. In time, clumsiness gives way to skill, skill to dexterity, and dexterity to something marvelous. So the practice of being aware of your movements is not difficult; simply lay down one rule for yourself: when you move, you must be aware. Keep at it, and you need not fear that the practice will fail to come to fruition.
Q: Sometimes delusive thoughts close in so completely that I cannot be aware of my movements at all. What then?

A: If that happens, just stop. Do not try to be aware of your movements; instead, calmly watch what your mind is thinking. The key to this practice is: first, watch it; second, pass no judgment on the content of what is thought (do not engage with it). Then delusive thoughts are like a fire that would burn the sky: after a while they go out. After that, return to being aware of your movements. If delusive thoughts close in again, do exactly the same. Nor is the time spent watching “what the mind is thinking” wasted, for you are training your ability to be aware of thoughts. Practiced in this way, the frequency and duration of delusive thoughts will fall sharply, and your awareness will grow steadily stronger. In fact, you should often look within and watch your own thoughts, emotions, and feelings — simply watching, without judgment. This is of great benefit for reducing delusive thoughts and cultivating awareness. Do it often enough and you will discover its subtle delight for yourself.
Q: When I am aware of my movements, a thought is present in my mind: “awareness.” Is that right or not?

A: When you are aware of your movements, it is right that the thought “awareness” is present in your mind; that is right mindfulness. Every thought other than this right mindfulness is a delusive thought. When you have practiced until “awareness” is the only thought left, you have achieved the gathering of all thoughts into one.
Q: What is eating Chan?

A: Eating Chan means making eating itself a practice of Chan. The method is to eat slowly, eat attentively, eat with awareness, chewing each mouthful at least thirty times and being aware of every chew. This not only cultivates awareness, dispels delusive thoughts, and lets you savor stillness, but also greatly aids digestion and absorption.
Q: Keeping awareness running without a break sounds easy — you need only not forget — yet I find it very hard to do. Where is the problem?

A: The problem lies in habit and in karmic obstruction. As for habit, you need only rid yourself of the old habit of heedlessness and form the new habit of clear and distinct knowing. But if the obstruction comes from karmic hindrance, examine whether you strictly uphold the five precepts and the ten good deeds, and repent of your karmic obstructions. Reciting one recitation of the Sutra of the Past Vows of Earth Store Bodhisattva each day and dedicating the merit is a most effective way to clear them away.

There is another effective method for keeping awareness running without a break: raise the huatou “just now.” First require of yourself that the huatou never break off — that is, raise the huatou “just now” at all times and in all places. On that basis, each time you raise the huatou “just now,” be aware of your present movement; if there is no movement, be aware of the present scene, a cup or a table, for instance. If your awareness is focused, you will discover something wonderful: the moment you raise the huatou and are at once aware of a movement or a scene, no delusive thought arises. In particular, once you have trained the method of “raise the huatou and be aware at once” to some depth, gathering all thoughts into one becomes very easy.

Feelings may be mental or physical, and the two are often closely joined. Emotions such as contentment and joy, craving and envy, dissatisfaction, suffering, resentment, blame, sorrow, depression, emptiness, fear, anxiety, and anger all give rise to feelings of body and mind.

Be aware of feelings, and be aware of whether you are clinging to them (taking them as real); then realize that feelings are illusory and impermanent and are not to be controlled by them: this is practice. And then
“he abides contemplating feelings as feelings, having put away covetousness and grief for the world, and dwells with awareness and clear comprehension alone”
(the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta).

To be aware of feelings is to observe and know them objectively, in the role of the observer, without judgment. Through awareness of feelings you can know your mind more precisely and can calm emotions and delusive thoughts. Be perfectly clear about how you feel right now.

To be aware of bodily and mental feelings without judgment not only releases negative emotions so that you are neither harmed nor controlled by them; it is also the perfect moment to uproot the seeds of karma. When an emotion produces a coarse or pricking sensation somewhere in the body, for example, gather your attention and be aware of that sensation until it vanishes. So whenever a negative emotion arises, at once be aware of it without judgment and observe the bodily and mental feelings it produces. The more you do this, the more promptly you will catch negative emotions without being harmed by them, and the more they will become aids to the bodhi path. When you are angry (or grieving), if you can observe it without judgment in the role of the observer, then although the anger (or grief) has not subsided, it can no longer control you.

Besides being promptly aware of the feelings that emotions produce and so escaping their control, in the course of daily life we can also cut off delusive thoughts and cultivate awareness by being aware of the feelings produced by our movements. The feeling of the body touching the bed as you sleep; of the body touching the chair or stool as you sit; of contact with the towel and water as you wash your face; of contact with the toothbrush as you brush your teeth; the many feelings of contact as you eat, wash the dishes, or walk. The benefits of doing this are two: first, no delusive thoughts; second, cultivation of awareness. If, while aware of a feeling, you are also aware of the movement that produced it, that is wonderful and fascinating, and the effect is still better — that is practice. By extension, in a single day you have many, many such opportunities for practice.

Through unremitting training, once you have mastered the arts of being aware of movement and being aware of feeling, then, as the Chan patriarchs said, putting on clothes and eating, carrying firewood and drawing water — none of it is other than practice. This is the key to making practice part of daily life.
In
the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta
the Blessed One taught:

Monks! And how does a monk abide contemplating feelings as feelings? Monks! When he experiences a pleasant feeling, he clearly knows: “I am experiencing a pleasant feeling.” When he experiences a painful feeling, he clearly knows: “I am experiencing a painful feeling.” When he experiences a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant, he clearly knows: “I am experiencing a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant.” When he clings to a pleasant feeling, he clearly knows: “I am clinging to a pleasant feeling.” When he does not cling to a pleasant feeling, he clearly knows: “I am not clinging to a pleasant feeling.” When he clings to a painful feeling, he clearly knows: “I am clinging to a painful feeling.” When he does not cling to a painful feeling, he clearly knows: “I am not clinging to a painful feeling.” When he clings to a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant, he clearly knows: “I am clinging to a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant.” When he does not cling to a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant, he clearly knows: “I am not clinging to a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant.”

In this way he abides contemplating feelings as feelings internally, he abides contemplating feelings as feelings externally, and he abides contemplating feelings as feelings both internally and externally. He abides observing the nature of arising in feelings, he abides observing the nature of vanishing in feelings, he abides observing the nature of both arising and vanishing in feelings. And so he clearly knows: “This is feeling!”
He dwells with awareness and clear comprehension alone,
“having put away covetousness and grief for the world.” Monks! This is how a monk abides contemplating feelings as feelings.
Q: I am often shrouded in negative emotions. What should I do?

A: Negative emotions are great enemies of body and mind. They not only make us suffer needlessly but also cause many illnesses. Look back over your own experience and you will see a fact: when you are shrouded in negative emotions, everything and everywhere goes wrong; when your heart is kind and your mind at ease, everything and everywhere goes well. So it is very important to detect negative emotions promptly and to release and dissolve them promptly.
Q: How can I release and dissolve negative emotions?

A: Observe them without judgment, be aware of the feelings they produce, and watch them with keen interest until this child who will not stop crying breaks into a smile. Note this, however: you must have a certain strength of awareness before these methods can work effectively. If you meet difficulties in applying them, then, as the previous chapter on “awareness of movement” explained, cultivate awareness further through being aware of your movements.
Q: How can I release tension and pressure?

A: Look within: where do tension and pressure come from? Keep looking, and you will enter a state in which there is no tension and no pressure. Then abide in that state, free of tension and pressure. Release tension and pressure in this way often, and they will not settle in and do their mischief.

Awareness of breathing is built on the preceding “awareness of movement” and “awareness of feeling.” So the more solid your earlier practice, the more easily this stage will come to hand. If you find awareness of breathing very difficult, you should go back and practice the earlier stages, and only when your awareness is sufficient begin to practice awareness of breathing. Every later stage likewise rests on the stage before it, so filling each hollow before moving on is the best and the fastest way.

[Fill each hollow before moving on] When a spring meets a hollow, it must fill it before it flows on. This likens learning to laying a firm foundation, advancing step by step, without impatience or reckless haste.

Awareness of breathing is subtler than awareness of movement, and breathing is present at every moment. To be aware of the breath at any time is most effective for raising awareness, and most beneficial to body and mind as well.

Because the purposes differ, there are very many ways of contemplating the breath. The awareness of breathing in this chapter serves Chan practice, so it differs from other contemplations. Two methods are introduced below; both are practiced in a still posture, with eyes open or closed as you please, and with no restriction on posture — sitting, lying down, or standing all will do; in both, the breath comes and goes through the nostrils. Of these three methods, choose one to practice; there is no need to practice them all.

The first method is to be aware of the breath at the tip of the nose (called, for short, contemplating the breath): breathe naturally, and when aware, do not trouble to distinguish the breath’s coming and going, its length, its heaviness or lightness, its slowness or speed; simply know that you are aware of the breath at the tip of the nose, and keep this state continuously, with the body relaxed. Its key phrase is: the eyes contemplate the nose. “The eyes contemplate the nose” means gathering the light of the eyes inward and turning it back to shine on the breath at the tip of the nose. (Note: never mistake “the eyes contemplate the nose” for looking at the tip of the nose with your eyes.) When your practice of contemplating the breath has deepened, the light of the spirit will come to rest at the tip of the nose, and you will be aware of the breath there at all times.

The second method is contemplating the breath by counting the breath: the tongue touches the upper palate, and the breathing is abdominal — breathe in deeply (the in-breath), and the abdomen gradually bulges; breathe out slowly (the out-breath), and the abdomen gradually recedes; and so it cycles. Take special care that the breathing be purely natural and that no force be used. As days pass and practice deepens, the breath will of itself become fine, deep, long, and slow. Before practicing, first relax body and mind, be serene and at ease, and even out the breath; then you may begin. On the out-breath, silently count six numbers: one, two, three, four, five, six. (Please note that this differs from the traditional method of counting the breath. In the traditional method, the first out-breath is counted as one, the second out-breath as two, and so on; in this method, however, six numbers — one, two, three, four, five, six — are counted on every out-breath.) On the in-breath, be aware of the inhalation; on the out-breath, be aware of each number as you count it, and let no stray thoughts arise. If stray thoughts do arise, that shows your awareness has scattered or been lost altogether; at once rouse yourself with a sharp jolt of awareness, gather your spirit, and begin again. When your practice of counting the breath has deepened, body and mind become still and composed, and the mind no longer takes pleasure in counting; then stop counting and focus on being aware of the in-breath and out-breath (contemplating the breath). In practice, should any state appear, good or bad, know that “all that has marks is delusive”: neither grasp nor reject it, neither delight nor grieve over it; keep your attention on being aware of the counting and of the breath, and you will not be harmed by it.

The third method is to be aware of the rising and falling of the abdomen: with abdominal breathing, the abdomen bulges on the in-breath and recedes on the out-breath, and the breathing should be natural. At the beginning, you may place a hand on the abdomen and feel its rising and falling. When your practice has matured and the mind gradually gathers, you can take the hand away and still be well aware of the rising and falling of the abdomen.
Furthermore, in studying awareness of breathing,
The Practical Practice of Vipassanā

is a book whose method is worth learning from; it takes awareness of the rising and falling of the abdomen as the core for cultivating awareness. For it borrows the basic exercises of Vipassanā to train a focused, continuous, and enduring awareness. So in using Vipassanā books, the essential thing is to read the basic exercises.

Awareness of breathing is a most important basic skill, and its uses are: first, to cultivate a focused, continuous, and enduring awareness; second, to train the mind, settling the scattered mind into stillness. The mind is like a wild elephant, frantic and destructive, and it must be tamed before its harm can be turned to benefit and it can work for us. Awareness of breathing is the taming of the mind; its mystery is hard to put into words, but if you keep practicing, once your skill has deepened a little you will realize that this is a wonderful method for stilling the mind and putting delusive thoughts to rest; hence the ancients likened it to a demon-slaying sword.

Awareness of breathing looks easy but is in fact quite difficult, because the attention is at any moment dragged away by delusive thoughts. So the remedy is: lost at once, recovered at once. That is, as soon as you notice that you have forgotten to be aware of the breath, bring the mind straight back and be aware of the breath attentively. Once the practice has come to hand, delusive thoughts are absent whenever you are aware of the breath. Deeper still: when delusive thoughts swirl, be attentively aware of the breath and they subside at once. This is the origin of the great name “demon-slaying sword.” Hence it is said: when delusive thoughts rise in swarms, contemplation of the breath is the anchor.
[Lost at once, recovered at once] The moment the mind strays, at once (immediately) bring it back.

The path of practice is this: discover, test, and sum up for yourself a method that lets awareness of breathing stand firm, stand long, and resist distraction. Ask yourself often: why did I forget to be aware of the breath? What plunged me into this delusive thought? As the saying goes, effort never betrays the willing heart. If your heart is sincere, your resolve firm, and you can endure hardship, and you keep practicing, the method will come of itself.

In this stage of practice, sit in awareness of the breath for at least two hours a day. For sitting meditation, the full lotus, half lotus, and cross-legged (loose) postures are all acceptable, and you may also sit upright on a chair or stool; the posture should keep the back straight (but do not thrust the chest out too far, and do not lean against the back of the chair) and be stable and enduring. Later, in the stages of “awareness of thoughts” and “Chan practice,” sitting practice must likewise be kept up for at least two hours a day — the more the better.

This practice of awareness of breathing is to be done not only sitting but also, and often, off the cushion: practice it standing, sitting, and lying down (walking and moving, practice awareness of movement), with eyes open and with eyes closed, seizing every spare moment to practice — practice! practice! practice!
Q: Some material on abdominal breathing says to hold the breath for
second after inhaling, and to hold it for
second after exhaling. May I use this method?
A: Yes, but do not lose awareness.
One point must be especially noted:
experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe in; experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe out. —
This is a very simple and direct and yet very effective method of practice. In the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta the Blessed One taught:

“He trains himself thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body’; he trains himself thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body.’ ... He dwells with awareness and clear comprehension alone, having put away covetousness and grief for the world.”
(See in full
the Commentary on the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta
(Beyond clinging) No habitual reaction arises.

blocks.text: Chapter Four: Awareness of the Present Moment

inline.s: The present moment is here and now.
To be present, wholly present, is to be one with this moment.
Not thinking of the past, not thinking of the future, live in the present moment.
Lose the present moment and the quality of your life will fall greatly.
What you do does not matter; what matters is that you do it while present.

To be aware of the present moment is to be aware of here and now. (Here is wherever the eyes and ears reach.) Its key point is this: toward everything around you, seeing is only seeing, hearing is only hearing, knowing is only knowing, perceiving is only perceiving — and no thought is stirred.

There was a practitioner named Bāhiya who, after a long journey, arrived travel-stained at Sāvatthī to seek the Dharma from the Buddha. He found the Buddha walking from house to house in the city, gathering alms, his every movement graceful and lovely, his six senses tamed and guarded, serene and still. Bāhiya bowed before him and begged the Buddha to teach him the Dharma, to teach him the Dharma of endless benefit and happiness. The Buddha said that he was now going from door to door for alms and that it was not the time to teach the Dharma. But Bāhiya asked again and again, and so the Buddha taught him the Dharma right there on the spot:

“Bāhiya, you should train yourself thus: in the seen there will be only the seen; in the heard, only the heard; in the known, only the known; in the perceived, only the perceived. Bāhiya, when you can do this — when in the seen there is only the seen, in the heard only the heard, in the known only the known, in the perceived only the perceived — then you have reached the end of clinging and obstruction. And if you have no clinging and no obstruction, then you have no past life and no future life. With no past and no future, these two
(and only the present moment)
, all sorrow, lamentation, pain, and grief are exhausted.”
(The original text is found in the Udāna of the Southern Transmission.)

[The three times] Past, present, and future. Any dharma that has arisen and ceased is called the “past”; any dharma that has arisen and not ceased is called the “present”; any dharma not yet arisen is called the “future.” [And only the present moment] The scripture says:
“In the seen there is only the seen, in the heard only the heard, in the known only the known, in the perceived only the perceived,”
and there is no delusive thought about past or future. In truth, people’s mental unease, anxiety, and suffering all arise from delusive thoughts about past or future.
To be aware without thinking, without a thought, is called presence.

It was said above that where there is awareness there are no floating thoughts; the “without thinking, without a thought” spoken of here means that not only are there no floating thoughts, but no thought is actively stirred either.
Keep the state of presence at all times and in all places. The Sutra of the Buddha Treasury says:
“The unsurpassed perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas is without thinking and without thought.”
The Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna says:
“What is called enlightenment means that the essence of mind is free from thought.”
(What is called enlightenment is the essence of mind free from thought.) The Essentials of Mind-Transmission says:
“Just as you are is it; stir a thought and you stray.” “Rest the thoughts, forget the cares, and the Buddha appears of himself.”
Chan Master Da’an said:
“If you
(you others)
would be Buddhas, then
(you need only be)
without all those minds of the multitude — inverted and clinging, deluded and evil notions, defiled desires and impurities — and you are the beginner’s right-enlightenment Buddha”
(the Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp)

You can train your ability to see only seeing by being aware of a flower, a tree, a bottle, a chair, and so on; and train your ability to hear only hearing by listening to music, the talk around you, the traffic in the street, the noise of machinery and appliances, and so on. Practice this often. Do it long enough and you will taste the wonder of “when the mind is gathered into one place, nothing is left undone.”

You may also be aware of the body or of some part of it — a finger, a toe, the palm, a knee, an arm, a shoulder, and so on. You may go further and be aware of your own nature, or be aware of the present moment. All of this is being aware of the present moment and so being present. The preceding three chapters (awareness of movement, awareness of feeling, awareness of breathing) and the chapter that follows (awareness of thoughts) are likewise awareness of the present moment, and so are presence.
Feeling the body from within will also bring you into presence.
In daily life, form the habit of doing everything consciously. Never do anything unconsciously!

A case was given above, but it bears repeating, because it matters so much. It is said that a fly came and settled on the Buddha’s face, and the Buddha lightly brushed it away with his hand. Then he made the gesture of brushing a second time. The disciples asked in wonder: “Blessed One, the first time you brushed it away was to drive off the fly; what was the second brushing for?” The Buddha answered: “The first was an unconscious movement, made without awareness, so I made the movement a second time with awareness, to correct it.” In this demonstration the Buddha teaches his disciples that every movement should be made consciously, with clear and distinct awareness, and that unconscious movement is ignorance and must be corrected at once.

Whenever a delusive thought arises, at once turn your attention to being aware of the present moment and being present. In that moment, simply attend to whether you are present, and pay no attention to how the delusive thought is doing. — In this way you can dismantle and dissolve delusive thoughts. (How hard or easy this is depends on the depth or shallowness of your practice of presence. So long as you keep at it, the wonder of it cannot be spoken.) Conversely, if you resent the delusive thought and want to drive it out and destroy it, you are fixing your attention on it, and it will only grow more solid and more ablaze.

Delusive thoughts are an alarm bell: when they ring, raise awareness at once and return to the present moment — be present, and stay present. Delusive thoughts are also sparring partners: whenever they come, use presence to dismantle them and dissolve them. This is how the power of presence is raised.

Q: I find presence a very easy and effective practice; it has solved a good many practical problems for me, including mental unease, anxiety, and suffering. I hope you will explain presence in more detail.
A:
Stones from another mountain may polish this one’s jade. To understand presence better, to experience it and apply it, you may read and watch:
The Power of Now
Stillness Speaks
How to Live Without Stress (video)
and
The Amazing Power of Yes (video)

. In reading and watching, note one thing: their author (Eckhart Tolle) holds that “consciousness” is the one ubiquitous essence in the universe, its supreme sovereign, and that the self is a part of consciousness or an embodiment of it. This differs from the Buddhadharma, and so it is called “another mountain.”
Q: How does one be aware of one’s own nature?

A: One’s own nature is the inner spiritual energy. To be aware of it is to feel it, to become one with it, and to abide in it. For sentient beings, the body is the dwelling of their own nature. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“The physical body is a house and dwelling.” Patriarch Linji said: “Just look at the puppets on the stage: the pulling of the strings depends wholly on the man inside.”
This means that the physical body is like a puppet, and what manipulates it is one’s own nature. The Formula for Cultivating the Mind says:
“When the hundred bones fall apart, they return to fire, return to wind; one thing remains ever living, covering heaven and covering earth.”

Throughout the twelve hours of the day, knowing hunger and thirst, knowing cold and heat, being angry or glad — this is one’s own nature. The physical body is a gathering of the four conditions, earth, water, fire, and wind; its substance is dull and insentient, so how could it see, hear, sense, and know? What can see, hear, sense, and know must be your own nature. The patriarch said:

“The four elements cannot explain the Dharma or hear the Dharma; empty space cannot explain the Dharma or hear the Dharma. Only that before your eyes, vividly and singly bright, without form or shape — that alone can explain the Dharma and hear the Dharma. What is without form or shape is your own nature.”
The Mahāyāna Lankāvatāra Sutra says:
“It is like a wooden man or a raised corpse
(causing a corpse to rise, walk, and move)
which stirs and turns and moves and acts
(does)
without cease, by the power of the mechanism of the piśāca.”

This means that the physical body is like a wooden man or a corpse, moving by the power of a mechanism. That mechanism is the life force of one’s own nature. To be aware of one’s own nature is to feel this living life force within the body, to become one with it, and to abide in it. Hold awareness of your own nature, and floating thoughts do not arise; you can then do without thought, or with single-minded thought, easily and naturally. To be aware of your own nature densely and without interruption is to be aware of and feel the living life force of your own nature within the body at all times and in all places, to become one with it, and to abide in it. In daily life, when conditions come, respond; when conditions go, be still. Whether at work or in conversation, keep awareness of your own nature, free and self-possessed (not falling into delusive thought, not controlled by conditions). The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“Not departing from one’s own nature is itself the field of blessing.”
Q: How does one be aware of the present moment?

A: To be aware of the present moment is to be deeply conscious of the present moment. When you are deeply conscious of the present moment, you are in a still state in which you do not think of the past or the future. Of course, you may also be aware of the present moment itself, that space which holds the arising of all things and events. When you are aware of this space, you are likewise in a still state in which you do not think of the past or the future.

Interviewed one cold winter’s day as he sat on a park bench, Eckhart Tolle said something most illuminating: “When you sit here, you just look at what is going on around you without any interpretation, just being with the situation as it is. You will then have some sense of what it is like to sit on a park bench. This moment, to which nothing need be added — sounds, sights, people, the sound of water, light and shadow — allow it to be just as it is. And that brings peace; you need not be forever caught up in events, thoughts, emotions, and reactions. You are the wider space in which all these things happen. You are the awareness behind all these things; without that awareness, none of this would be here — in space there would be only atoms and molecules. You are the awareness that allows the whole world to be; the awareness that can understand is who you truly are — not by thinking in concepts, but through direct realization. Step back and allow the phenomenal world to be just as it is, allow this moment to be just as it is. This will take you deeper into yourself, and you may then find a sudden stillness in the background; it just happens. Yet you must be alert; you need to stay alert, alert to the situation as it is, alert to your senses and sensations and to the energy behind the feelings — that is, awareness. Be alert. Without alertness you drift into thinking and start thinking about the next thing: what will happen to me tomorrow? There is a place for making plans, but it is not on a park bench. This is not the place to think about how tomorrow should be, for you will miss all the beauty and vitality around you (laughs). And then you feel cold, but you need not even think that what you feel is “cold.” Yes, it is simply a sensation; you need not call it “cold.” Even that is fine, no problem; there are no longer conditioned reactions in life — always resisting, always opposing something, always wanting to grasp at something.”
(from
“Eckhart Tolle: Enlightenment in the Present Moment (video)”
Q: How does one practice “a mirror reflecting things”?
A: Be aware of the present scene without thinking and without a thought. Master Yinguang said:

“If you would have true knowledge appear, then in your daily activities always raise the light of awareness, and let no irrational thought or feeling so much as sprout in the mind. Keep the mind always empty and bright and thoroughly clear. Like a mirror on its stand, it reflects whatever appears; it only reflects the scene before it, and does not follow the scene and turn. Beauty and ugliness are their own affair — what has that to do with me? What comes, do not plan for in advance; what goes, do not cling to. If some irrational thought or feeling so much as stirs, attack and cure it severely, and wipe it out utterly.”
(Preface to the Four Lessons of Liao-Fan; for a full annotated explanation see
Annotated Four Lessons of Liao-Fan: Summary of the Original Preface
Q: When I am present, may I keep the mind on the dantian and cultivate both nature and life?

A: Yes. And if, while present, you keep the mind on the jiaji point, the effect will be still better. The jiaji, also called the jiaji double pass, is the xinshu point. For the effects of keeping the mind on the jiaji, see in full

Seize every present moment of the mind.

To be aware of thoughts is to know your own mind. The mind spoken of here is the thought that arises when the six sense faculties meet the six sense objects. A practitioner must know his own thoughts at all times — when raising troops to put down bandits, one should know where the bandits are. And the importance of contemplating the mind goes far beyond this.

Patriarch Bodhidharma’s Treatise on Breaking the Marks says: “The single Dharma of contemplating the mind gathers up all dharmas and is the most essential and concise.” The Mahāyāna Sutra of the Contemplation of the Mind Ground says: “Within the three realms, the mind is sovereign; one who can contemplate the mind attains ultimate liberation, and one who cannot remains forever in bondage.” It also says: “This Dharma (contemplating the mind) is called the supreme secret mind-ground Dharma-door of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions; it is called the Dharma-door of sudden enlightenment by which all ordinary beings enter the Tathāgata’s ground; it is called the true straight path by which all bodhisattvas advance to great bodhi; it is called the wondrous jewel palace in which the Buddhas of the three times enjoy the bliss of the Dharma; it is called the inexhaustible treasury of all that benefits sentient beings.” It also says: “If one can cultivate this profound and wonderful contemplation, the fruit of delusion, karma, and suffering cannot arise; only contemplate the true mark, the nature of suchness, and both subject and object are forgotten, all views transcended.” The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “All Tathāgatas, from the ground of their original arising, rely on perfect illumination of the pure mark of enlightenment, forever cutting off ignorance, and only then accomplish the Buddha way.” The Nirvāṇa Sutra says: “To be able to contemplate the nature of the mind is called supreme samādhi.”

Master Taixu, in his Lecture Notes on the Mahāyāna Sutra of the Contemplation of the Mind Ground, said: “(This sutra) points out to Mahāyāna practitioners the awakening of the will — this is the most reliable and practical Dharma-door.” “Although this sutra has as many as thirteen chapters, the ‘Chapter on Contemplating the Mind’ is especially important. If a practitioner can contemplate the mind and know that the mind is illusory and still, he will not be deluded and clinging; when clinging is gone, deluded confusion cannot arise; when confusion does not arise, wisdom grows; when wisdom grows, afflictions are destroyed; confusion destroyed and wisdom born — this is of practical use to the practitioner, and completes the virtue of severance.”

[The six faculties] Eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. [The six sense objects] Objects of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects. “Object” means defilement: they can defile people’s pure minds and keep the true nature from revealing itself. The six sense objects are also called the six fields, that is, the fields perceived by the six faculties. [The virtue of severance] All afflictions cut off, pure and unconditioned, free and at ease. This is one of the Buddha’s three virtues. The Buddha’s three virtues are the virtue of wisdom, the virtue of grace, and the virtue of severance.

Awareness of thoughts has three links: first, seeking back the strayed mind; second, knowing without following; third, not departing from the present thought. Of these, “knowing without following” is the central link that joins what comes before to what comes after.
To be aware of the present moment is called the mind being present; this is enlightenment. To fall into delusive thought is for the mind to be absent; this is delusion. Mencius said:
“When a man’s chickens and dogs stray, he knows to seek them; but when his mind strays, he does not know to seek it. The way of learning is nothing else: it is simply seeking back the strayed mind.”
(the Mencius,

Gaozi chapter) (Paraphrase: some people know to go and look for a lost chicken or dog, yet when their mind is lost they do not know to go and look for it. The learning of being human is nothing else: it is simply finding that lost mind again.)
[The way of learning] “Learning” here does not mean systematic knowledge, but the cultivation of mind and nature, the learning of how to be human.

The mind being present means the mind is aware of the present moment. To draw back the mind that has fallen into the world of the head (delusive thought) and be aware of the present moment (this time, this place, this matter) — to live in the present moment — this is the first step in awareness of thoughts. The ordinary person’s mind is like a wild horse, a mad elephant, a cunning ape; it cannot be governed at all, and is always in delusive thought. To draw the mind back is to step out of the world of the head (delusive thought); this is a most important step — what is called “when the mind is gathered into one place, nothing is left undone.” Conversely, if the mind is scattered, nothing can be accomplished. Practice is the cultivation of the mind: if the mind is scattered, all the practice one does is empty, like the showy but useless postures spoken of in the martial arts.

So you must take your own thoughts in hand. Attend to your thoughts at all times and in all places; if they stray, draw them back at once and keep them in the present moment. Keep doing the work of gathering the mind back: lost at once, recovered at once. There are many ways to gather the mind; you can try them out and find the one that suits you best.

Here is one method: question yourself in self-reflection, “Master, is the mind present?” At once turn the light around and look to see whether your mind has strayed; as you look carefully, the mind is drawn back, and you answer yourself, “Present.” This is a most interesting practice. Do it often, and when the practice deepens the mind will settle; even if it strays, a single sharp jolt of awareness brings it back.

Huike (later the Second Patriarch of Chan) came to Patriarch Bodhidharma and said: “My mind is not at peace; I beg you, Master, to set my mind at peace.” Bodhidharma said: “Bring me your mind, and I will set it at peace for you.” Huike said: “I have sought the mind, and it is utterly unobtainable.” Bodhidharma said: “I have set your mind at peace for you.”

This is the wondrous method of setting the mind at peace handed down by Patriarch Bodhidharma: seeking the mind. When thoughts disturb you, look closely at the thought and see what it actually wants; the thought then stops of itself, and the mind comes to rest — what is called “contemplate the thought and the thought at once stops (ceases).” (This wondrous method of setting the mind at peace is most effective. If you still cannot take it up, or find it very hard going, it shows that your awareness is not yet strong enough; set it aside for the time being and take it up again when your awareness is stronger.)
Through constant practice, once you have the beginnings of a foundation in gathering the mind back, a single reminder to yourself — just now! — and the mind is drawn back.

Observe often: is the mind present, or has it strayed? If the mind is in the present moment — that is, on this time, this place, or this matter (what you are doing) — then it is present; if the mind is thinking delusively of another time, another place, or another matter, then it has strayed; draw it back at once, and do “dressing is just dressing, eating is just eating,” aware of the present moment.
With one mind he thinks a swan is coming” — this is the classic case of delusive thinking. The Mencius,

Gaozi I, says: “Yi Qiu was the finest chess player in the whole country. Suppose Yi Qiu teaches two men to play chess. One of them concentrates wholly, listening only to Yi Qiu; the other, though he listens, has his whole mind on a swan he thinks is coming and wants to fetch bow and arrow to shoot it. Though he studies with the other, he does not equal him. Is it because his intelligence is not equal? I say: no, it is not so.” (Paraphrase: Yi Qiu was the finest chess player in the country. Let Yi Qiu teach two men to play chess. One of them concentrates wholly, listening only to Yi Qiu’s teaching and thinking of nothing else; the other, though he listens, keeps thinking that a swan is about to fly over and wants to take bow and arrow and shoot it. Thus, though taught by the same teacher, he learns less than the first. Can one say that his intelligence is not equal to the other’s? I say: it is not so.)

Originally, our thinking exists to serve our survival in this world of forms. So thought should be like tap water: turn it on when you need it, turn it off when you do not. It should also be like a servant, wholly obedient to the sovereign’s command, with no presumption to act on its own. But the present situation is exactly the opposite: thought is domineering and willful, it controls you, and it only turns on and never stops, phantasy following phantasy and delusive thoughts swirling. Practice means the master takes back the great power and makes thought obey you. In the Sutra of the Buddha’s Bequeathed Teaching the Buddha says: “The mind is more to be feared than a venomous snake, a savage beast, or a robber; a runaway great fire is no fit simile for it. It is like a man holding a vessel of honey, who moves about heedlessly, seeing only the honey and not the deep pit. It is like a mad elephant without a hook, or a monkey that has gained a tree, leaping and springing beyond all restraint. You must strike it down at once and not let it run loose. Indulge this mind and one loses all good works; gather it to one place and nothing is left undone. Therefore, monks, be diligent and strive, and tame your minds.”

The mind being present means the mind is on this time, this place, or this matter (what one is doing), with no clinging or delusive thought. “The mind being present” has two cases: one is the mind in a state of work, the other is the mind in a state of stillness. When life or business requires the mind to work, the mind is in a state of work, and should then think with whole concentration; when the mind is not needed for work, it should be in a state of stillness, without thought or notion, and must never let phantasies run on. So the work of “the mind being present” should be done from these two sides.

Then how can the mind be wholly concentrated when it works, and how can it be without thought or notion when it is still? Since this book is entirely about practice, it lays stress on how the mind can be without thought or notion. The Sutra of the Buddha Treasury says: “The unexcelled perfect enlightenment of all dharmas is without thought and without notion.” The Essentials of Mind-Transmission says: “Rest the thoughts, forget the cares, and the Buddha appears of himself.” As for how to achieve the wholly concentrated presence of mind in Chan practice or mind contemplation, that is discussed in detail in the relevant chapters.

There are many ways for the mind to reach the state of no thought and no notion; here we focus on the method of being aware of the present moment. When you are attentively aware of the present moment (deeply conscious of this moment), the mind is in the state of no thought and no notion. For floating thoughts all run to what is before and behind, having nothing to do with the present moment, and their aim is to drag you away from it. So in this section, train hard at being aware of the present moment (the mind being present). Be aware of the present moment from thought to thought without a break, until movement and stillness become one piece, and keep the numinous terrace clear and bright. Clear means no thought; bright means awareness.
[The numinous terrace] Refers to the mind, the heart.

The past has already passed, the future has not yet come; all you can possess is this one present moment, and the quality of this moment truly shapes your future. So to place all your attention on this present moment — the mind being present — is of the utmost importance. This is why the Chan patriarchs always taught people to live in the present moment.

To cultivate a focused, continuous, and enduring awareness is of the utmost importance. In the work of “the mind being present,” be present with focus, be present continuously, be present enduringly. In a word: focused, continuous, and enduring presence of mind!
Q: I am attentively aware of the present moment, yet delusive thoughts still come without end. What should I do?

A: This shows that your awareness is not yet strong enough. You should strengthen the earlier stages — awareness of movement, awareness of feeling, and awareness of breathing — and only when the foundation is solid begin the practice of “awareness of thoughts.”

What is called “the mind being present” is the mind focused on what is seen, heard, or done, with no other thought. This is the key to “dressing and eating are also practice.” Grasp this key, and you can practice at all times and in all places. Then you not only have ample time for practice and can attend to both work and practice, but your practice runs without interruption, and accomplishment comes easily.

When your practice deepens, you will find that “the mind being present” is most wonderful and full of interest; this is the realm of Chan. Check at all times: is the mind present? The moment you check, the mind settles. Practice it in leisure, in work, in waiting, in restlessness and agitation.

A student asked Chan Master Zhaozhou: what should a person who has understood the mind and seen the nature be like? Master Zhaozhou answered: he should practice greatly all the more. The student said: I wonder whether a master of your attainment still practices? Master Zhaozhou said: I just put on clothes and eat. The student said: putting on clothes and eating are ordinary things — can this too be practice? Master Zhaozhou said: if it were not practice, then tell me, what do I do every day? (Original text: “Q: What of the man who has finished the matter? The Master said: He practices greatly. The student said: I wonder whether the Master still practices? The Master said: Putting on clothes and eating. The student said: Putting on clothes and eating are ordinary things; I wonder whether this is practice? The Master said: Then tell me, what do I do every day?” — the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhaozhou)

Master Hanshan said: “Someone asked: ‘The ancients ate when hungry and slept when tired, and that was the Way. People today eat when hungry and sleep when tired — why is that not the Way?’ The answer: ‘The ancients, eating, only ate; sleeping, only slept, and so it was the Way. People today, eating, do not eat; sleeping, do not sleep, (but) run on in wild imagining and reckoning, and so they turn their backs on the Way.’ From this we see that in your daily round you need only lift your eyebrows, give a shout, and make gods start and ghosts fear, make the heavenly demons’ gall burst and the dark spirits’ souls melt; one shout drives them all back, and you are left with the ground of your own place, silent and still, not a thread hanging, bare and naked. Take this one family style, and when you want to read, read; when you do not, set it aside and do not hang a single word on it. When you want to write, write; when you do not, set it aside and do not indulge in wild reckoning. Even drinking tea and eating rice — just drink tea and eat rice; when you want to sleep, sleep; when you must relieve yourself, relieve yourself. Whatever you meet, be done with it, and never allow yourself to brood over it afterward. Be like a wandering ghost, clean and pure, spotless and white — and do not sit down inside the clean and spotless white (do not lose the light of awareness and fall into blankness). Thus, single-edged and straight in, with one thought forward, reading you see the ancients face to face, and writing you spit it out in one mouthful from your own breast, with no before and after. When you are storing it up, that is the moment of pouring it out; when you are pouring it out, that is the moment of storing it up. In this way you are not turned about by movement and stillness, light and dark, nor shifted by any manner of trick.”(the Dream Roaming Collection,
Instruction to Huang Weiheng)
Q: When I do the work of gathering the mind back, the mind comes back, but I cannot keep it; it runs off again at once, and I watch it run with my own eyes and am helpless. What should I do?

A: When the mind has been drawn back, you must tether it with awareness; this is usually called guarding the mind. For example, do one thing with whole concentration (especially the small trifles of daily life — the best objects for practice), with the mind nowhere else and perfectly clear; or be aware of your movements, your feelings, your breathing, the present moment; or be aware of a flower, a tree, an object, without stirring a thought — like a mirror reflecting things, fixing the mind on one place. So the key to guarding the mind is: be aware of it and stir no thought. The work of gathering and guarding the mind rests on the earlier cultivation of awareness; if, when you gather the mind, you find your awareness not yet strong enough, so that you cannot draw it back (caught in the world of delusive thought and unable to pull free), or can draw it back but cannot keep it, then strengthen the practice of the preceding four stages (awareness of movement, awareness of feeling, awareness of breathing, and awareness of the present moment).
Q: I often lie in bed with delusive thoughts swirling. What should I do?

A: If this happens, at once be aware of your breathing, or be aware of movement or feeling or the present moment. You may, for instance, use the finger-twirling method: slowly and repeatedly rub and twirl (stroke) the middle and index fingers with the thumb, attentively aware of each movement and of the sensation of contact between the fingers, the mind following the fingers. When this practice is familiar, body and mind enter easily into a state both serene and still and aware. Whenever and wherever delusive thinking goes on and on, that is a wretched thing: it is delusion, it is dreaming the dream of saṃsāra. At such a time, at once rouse yourself with a sharp jolt of awareness and draw the mind back, focusing on what you are doing; or be aware of your breathing, or of movement, or of feeling; or be aware of the present moment: dwell in the present with everything around you and stir no thought, so that circumstances do not disturb the mind and the mind does not run after circumstances. Do this often and you will grope your way to a whole set of methods that keep you in the state of awareness, abiding in the present moment.

The method of being aware of thoughts is: observe your own thoughts without judging them. This point of “without judging” is very important, for otherwise you will breed delusion upon delusion. Its key is: know it, but do not follow it.
The Treatise on the Awakening of the Bodhi Mind says:
“If a deluded mind arises
(if a delusive thought arises)
, know it and do not follow it; when the delusion ceases
(when the delusive thought ceases)
, the source of mind is empty and still, and all virtues are complete, with wondrous function inexhaustible.”

[Knowing without following] Watch the thought without judging it, and do not let it continue (do not breed thought upon thought). The key to “knowing without following” is to work at the “knowing,” watching as a cat watches a mouse hole, so that the moment a thought arises you know it. Once you can “know the moment a thought arises,” “not following” becomes easy. [Source of mind] The mind is the source of all dharmas, hence “source of mind.” [All virtues are complete] All virtues are complete. “Are” here means “then.” For example: with preparation, one can then be free of trouble.

When you are aware of your thoughts and observe your thinking, you experience the presence of the master — it is the master who is aware of thoughts and observes thinking. This master is you; thinking is not you. When a thought arises and you run after it, it controls you, and you may even take it to be yourself. If a thought arises and you do not run after it but know it without following it, then you are the master. This is freedom — to exist autonomously. From beginningless kalpas, sentient beings have been deluded and inverted, running after thoughts, giving rise to confusion and creating karma, so that birth and death and saṃsāra never cease. Now, to end birth and death and escape saṃsāra, the urgent task is to break free of the head’s control and be a free person.
